newsitem.title: INDIA: India keen on resumption of talks with Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: India keen on resumption of talks with Pakistan.

text.p: India said on Tuesday it is hopeful of better ties with arch-rival Pakistan under a new government led by Nawaz Sharif, but analysts cautioned they did not foresee a radical change in Islamabad's foreign policy.

India's Foreign Ministry said it hoped the new Pakistan government would respond to an offer made by Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to restart talks between senior officials shortly after he took office in June 1996.
"Let the new Pakistan government be sworn in and we will wait for a response," Talmiz Ahmed, a foreign ministry spokeman, told a news conference.

India was interested in holding an official dialogue with Pakistan on all issues, Ahmed said. "We have had no response so far. We hope the new government will give a response...We would welcome a resumption of the dialogue between two countries if Pakistan wants it."
The Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif appeared headed for a crushing victory over Benazir Bhutto in Monday's national election.
Pakistan President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government last November accusing it of corruption and misrule.
Latest results show Sharif's party has secured 116 seats of the 161 results declared in the 217-member National Assembly while Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party is straggling in with nine seats.

"There is hope that normal dialogues will be revived under Nawaz Sharif not immediately but over a six-month period," Brahma Chellaney, an analyst with Centre for Policy Research, a private think-tank, told Reuters.
Carved out of British India in 1947 in a bloodstained partition of the subcontinent, India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over troubled the Kashmir region.
The neighbours have not held official talks for more than three years, mainly because of deep differences over Kashmir.
Pakistan has said it wants Kashmiris to be able to vote in a plebiscite to determine their future. India, which rules over two-thirds of the Himalayan region, says the issue is strictly internal.
All government offices in Pakistan will be closed on Wednesday to demonstrate support for Kashmiri militants.

Pakistan denies Indian charges of training and arming the Kashmiri militants, but Pakistani foreign minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan said on Tuesday that Pakistan would "continue to extend all moral, political and diplomatic support to their struggle against Indian occupation".
Indian commentators said Bhutto, during her tenure as prime minister, did little to improve bilateral relations.

"Bhutto proved to even more aggressive than her predecessors and, as a result, the relations between the two countries deteriotated to an extent not seen before in times of peace," an editorial in Tuesday's Hindustan Times newspaper said.
Analysts noted that Sharif, during his earlier prime ministership between 1990 to 1993, had held several meetings with then Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"During his election campaign Sharif made suggestions to improve bilateral relations through dialogue," said J.N. Dixit, a former Indian foreign secretary.
"We should be responsive to suggestions made by Sharif on normalisation of relations," Dixit said.
But Chellaney said so far as broad foreign policy was concerned there were unlikely to be major changes.
"Not many changes in the overall foreign policy are foreseen," he said. "The main question is to clean up the (Pakistan) economic situation."
